L23: ## About us
L24: Payers now run AI that reviews, adjusts, and denies claims faster than any practice can keep up with by hand, and a lot of what a practice is owed quietly slips away. 53% of patients with a denied claim never appeal it. Altair is the AI medical billing service for independent practices The AI does the work, backed by our expert in-house billers, so there is no billing operation for you to staff, manage, or chase.
L25: Before the visit, Altair clears eligibility, prior authorization, and pre-determination the way each payer requires. Before a claim ships, Altair checks it against that payer's own policies, so it goes out clean and compliant the first time. When a denial lands, Altair works it and files the appeal based on how that payer behaves, then bills the patient and posts the cash. Altair learns the payers’ behaviour with every claim and forecasts what you will be paid.
L26: Altair puts every claim, dollar, denial, and appeal in one live view, so you always know where your money stands. Altair tracks each payer's policies as they change, plugs into the EHR and clearinghouse you already use with no rip and replace, and is HIPAA compliant. The longer Altair runs your billing, the fewer denials come back, and the harder it becomes for payers to deny you. Payers have AI. Now so do you.

L88: When someone appeals a denied health insurance claim, they win most of the time. About eight times out of ten. You'd think that would make people appeal everything. Almost no one does. Barely one in nine even tries. A system this wrong should be losing. It keeps winning because every denial is a bet that you won't fight back. Three things make that bet safe. The first is speed. At one large insurer, the doctors signing off on denials spent about a second on each.
L89: A computer flags the claim, a human signs the batch, and the no goes out before you finish this sentence. Undoing it takes a person, on hold, for an afternoon. The cheap side wins on volume. The second is friction. You resubmit, they want the records. You send the records, they want a peer-to-peer call. Six months pass, and the patient's coverage has lapsed. In a normal business, friction costs you customers. Here it keeps your money on their side another month, or twelve. The friction is the product.
L90: It only has to make fighting cost more than the claim is worth. Chasing one denied claim can cost around $57, and plenty are worth less. So no one chases them. The third is accountability. Fight all the way through to a person on the phone, and they can't reverse the decision. You're talking to the one person guaranteed to have no power to act. At one insurer, staff were told to keep their decisions within one percent of what the algorithm predicted. None of this is new.
L91: What's new is that each factor used to have a ceiling, because saying no still took a person. AI took the ceiling off all three. Saying no used to be cheap. Now it's free, and it runs on every claim, every patient. In 2026, Medicare itself started paying outside companies to screen care with AI, based on how much they cut its spending. The more care they hold back, the more they keep. They're paid, by contract, to say no. The usual response is to hire more people. You can't out-hire a machine.
L92: When saying no costs almost nothing, the only move is to make fighting back cost almost nothing too. Most people think AI just means doing the old job faster. Bolt it onto a broken process and you only speed up the mess. Your bot appeals, their bot denies, and as one researcher put it, you make the system more efficient at being expensive. The real answer is a different operating system. Every denial is born in the gap between your clinical record and the insurer's rules.
L93: An AI-native system closes that gap. It carries the rules inside the claim before it goes out, so there's nothing left to deny. When a denial slips through, you answer it at machine speed, not from a chair on hold. That shift is the line between the practices that stay independent and the ones that get acquired or shut down. For twenty years, the safest bet in American healthcare has been that you'd give up the fight.
L94: We built Altair so the people who actually show up for patients are the ones left standing.

L65: 【20†Antropi Robotics (YC F26)】 is building autonomous factories that make inspected CNC parts for hardware teams in days instead of weeks. CNC machines already cut metal automatically, but people still need to plan jobs, load machines, inspect parts, and handle problems. Antropi’s Factory OS connects these steps into one system. Its first factory is live and already shipping parts to customers with lead times under 7 days.
L66: The goal is a network of autonomous factories across the US that make and deliver parts locally in as little as 24 hours. Founders 【21†Naman Gupta†www.linkedin.com】 and 【22†Shubh Agarwal†www.linkedin.com】 have been building hardware together since college in 2017. Naman was the first employee and Chief of Staff at Accio Robotics before running his dad’s CNC machining business. Shubh completed his Master’s in Robotics at the University of Pennsylvania, working with robotic manipulators.
L67: They’ve experienced this problem from both sides: waiting for parts and running the factory that makes them. Need CNC parts? Order here: 【23†www.antropi.shop†www.antropi.shop】 Congrats on the launch, Naman and Shubh! 🚀 【24†https://lnkd.in/gCuTxGun†lnkd.in】

L76: 🏭 We’re building factories that run themselves. Our founders still delivered this order in person. 【21†Naman†www.linkedin.com】 and 【22†Shubh†www.linkedin.com】 hand-delivered our first order to 【26†Pave Robotics†www.linkedin.com】 as we ramp up deliveries to hardware teams in the US. It was a chance to understand what matters beyond the drawing: how the parts will be used, what slows the team down, and what would make their next build easier. Parts that fit. Delivery dates you can trust.
L77: Prices that let you keep building. That’s what autonomous factories should change. Not just how a part is made, but how easy it is for someone to build with it. Our goal: US quality, China prices, delivered in under 24 hours. We’re working toward a network of factories running 24/7, close to the teams that need them. The exciting part isn’t just faster parts. It’s what happens when every design change no longer means weeks of waiting.
L78: Teams can test more ideas, improve faster, and build things they might otherwise never attempt. More robots. More drones. More rockets. We’re excited about the parts we’re making. Even more excited about what people will build with them. 🚀

Machines wait on people, quality gets checked at the end, and even simple parts take weeks.
